title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
authors: Govind Velamoor; Adrian Lin; Sam Jung; Spencer Mateega; Brandon Y. Yang; Amish Sethi
abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. authors: Haozhe Zhang; Gu Zhang; Zirui Zou; Yuzheng Chen; Jinlong Wu; Zixuan Hu
abstract: Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework for human-to-robot data transformation. authors: Neel Jawale; Stephan Pleines; Soha Pouya; Yuke Zhu; Ajay Mandlekar; Caelan Garrett
abstract: Multi-arm robot platforms, including bimanual and humanoid robots, have the capability to complete tasks with lower cycle times than single-arm systems, but they are more difficult to safely control due to the presence of multi-arm constraints. authors: Xin Ma; Furong Chen; Xinlong Man; Bo Zhang; Yalong Guo; Haolan Lei
abstract: Choosing a robot action model requires evidence about task capability, adaptation cost, deployment requirements, and the reliability of reported conclusions. authors: Junli Liu; Zhongrui You; Chenhui Li; Zhen Li; Yuyang Tian; Qizhen Chen
abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. authors: Jianming Ma; Rongjun Jin; Yizhi Chen; Yue Gao
abstract: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. abstract: Agentic robots must turn a high-level goal into actions while keeping the physical conditions needed for future steps valid. A completed action does not ensure that its effects will persist: a later disturbance can invalidate support that the remaining plan still assumes. authors: Jingxu Gu; Dongze Lian
abstract: Fine-grained manipulation requires a robot policy to follow instructions, remain robust to visual variations, and translate predicted actions into precise robot control. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. authors: Pranjal Aggarwal; Sean Welleck
abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. authors: Yixue Zhang; Wenke Xia; Kun Wu; Wenbo Yu; Pei Ren; Junnan Nie
abstract: Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) to guide action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them. authors: Jonathan Yang; Chelsea Finn; Dorsa Sadigh
abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? authors: Rufeng Xiao; Ruihao Xiao; Wei Chen; Xinhai Sun
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn to predict representations rather than pixels, offering a compact way to model how visual scenes evolve. abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but lowering bit widths while maintaining task performance remains challenging. abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. authors: Guoning Wu; Zijian Cai; Yuhang Zhang; Ying Liu; Yongbin Zheng
abstract: Multi-robot control requires integrating distributed camera views while predicting separate action sequences. Most vision-language-action and world-action models target one robot. authors: Marc Ziegler; Batu Özen; Sami Mentes; Thomas Waschulzik; Alois Knoll
abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. authors: Haoyu Zhao; Xingyue Zhao; Zhian Su; Bohan Hou; Yinzhou Tang; Fengyi Wang

authors: Jie Wang; Bo Zhang; Renzhi Lu; Jianyu Chen

abstract: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. authors: Luai Abuelsamen

authors: Enfu Nan; Pu Zhao; Yixiao Chen; Lin Zhao; Juyi Lin; Chen Wang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to follow instructions in typed text, limiting broader deployment in natural speech. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. authors: Vigneshwaran Subbaraju; Obaidullah Zaland; Monowar Bhuyan

authors: Xi Chen; Fengqi Hu; Zeyu Shen; Jiaying Xu; Shangding Gu; Pan Xu
abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. authors: Seungyong Moon; Deokjae Lee; Hansang Lee; Munkhtselmeg Battsengel; Youngin Kim; Seonghyeon Yun
abstract: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. authors: Jiachi Yang; Zhiyi Xu; Hongquan Zhang; Xin Tan; Zhizhong Zhang; Jingyu Gong

authors: Thomas Landeg; Thierry Tambe
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. authors: Minho Park; Kinam Kim; Donghu Kim; Byungkun Lee; Dongyoon Hwang; Yongjae Shin
abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions, but their large weight footprint challenges deployment on memory-constrained onboard platforms. authors: Borui Xu; Han Chen; Bingsheng He; Ming Wu; Jason Zeng; Michael Heinrich
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer knowledge from large-scale pretraining into robot control, but their manipulation performance remains sensitive to changes in observation conditions, which recent work addresses by fine-tuning the visual module on target-domain data. authors: Haocheng Wang; Youquan Liu; Weiyu Guo; Aokai Zhang; Donghang Wu; Hongyu Liu

authors: Matthew Strong; Ankush K. Dhawan; Julien Poffet; Giuse Pham; Jinho So; Monroe Kennedy
abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. authors: Matteo Cercola; Katie Z Luo; Simone Formentin; Marco Pavone
abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. authors: Zhan Yi; Yuchen Wang; Chao Li; Lei Hong; Boyuan Yang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. authors: Xiaoxu Xu; Hao Li; Hongtao Zhang; Yili Tang; Jiafei Cao; Junhao Cai
abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. authors: Jiatong Li; Jisheng Dang; Qiangqiang Ma; Bimei Wang; Jingwen Zhao; Wenjun Ma
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. authors: Jingjiao Zhao; Dong Jing; Mingyu Cao; Ruochuan Shi; Xiansheng Chen; Pengwei Wang
abstract: History-dependent robotic manipulation requires task context and interaction history, as the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the next action. Hierarchical frameworks use task memory for high-level subgoal reasoning and low-level policies for execution. authors: Daniel Weiner; Raj Korpan
abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. authors: Xinxin Liu; Bingxin Xu; Wenrui Bao; Ming Li; Wentao Bao; Chen Chen
abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode. abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. authors: Song-Li Wu; Chubin Zhang; Wenbo Ding; Yansong Tang
abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. authors: Hamid Hafezi; Javad Mohammadpour Velni; Mohammadreza Davoodi
abstract: Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. authors: Jiaming Liu; Xinghao Zhu; Yiming Zhang; Shanghang Zhang; Yinxi Wang; Yichu Yang
abstract: Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. abstract: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. authors: Colton Crosby; Hao Wang; Mac Schwager; Somil Bansal
abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. authors: Peidong Wang; Ying Chang; Zhiming Ma; Xiaocui Yang; Shi Feng; Daqi Liu
abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. authors: Liqian Ma; Vaibhav Saxena; Utkarsh Aashu Mishra; Shuo Cheng; Yongxin Chen; Danfei Xu
abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. authors: Junhoo Lee; Seungyeon Kim; Baekseung Kim; Minkyu Kim; Suhyun Jeon; Jimyeong Kim
abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation
authors: Hiroki Nishizawa; Takehiko Ohkawa; Nicola Scianca; Tatsuya Matsushima; Shigeo Morishima; Kei Ota
abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. authors: Shangqing Zhou; Zhennan Jiang; Ning Ma; Xin Fu; Yupeng Zheng; Shuai Tian
abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. authors: Mingxuan Yan; Litian Gong; Dihong Huang; Zhixu Li; Tianyu Zhang; Wenqian Zhang
abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. authors: Haomin Wang; Anqiong Ji; Ke Wang; Zhongshan Liu; Ru Ying; Ran Zheng
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. authors: Yiqing Xu; Jiajun Wu
abstract: A robot may know how to perform a task yet fail when a human asks for it naturally. authors: Jack Lu; Yurong You; Boyi Li; Yulong Cao; Thomas Tian; Chaowei Xiao
abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. title: TRACE: Efficient Transfer Learning for Neural Whole-Body Control Across Humanoid Embodiments
authors: Qingyu Lan; Zhihao Tian; Zifan Wang; Junwei Liang
abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
authors: Xinyi Wang; Bangzheng Li; Hanyu Wang; Lin Zhang; Andrea Yaoyun Cui; Zhenggang Tang
abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? authors: Maria Attarian; Yifan Ruan; Claas Voelcker; Chenyang Cao; Amy Zhang; Peter Stone
abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. authors: Chang Liu; Sibo Tian; Litian Gong; Zhiwen Fan; Jiachen Li; Xiao Liang
abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
authors: Wenxuan Guo; Yingping Liang; Zhaoguo Wang; Ziyuan Li; Angyuan Ma; Zhenyu Wu
abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui; Hanyu Wang; Xinyi Wang; Bangzheng Li; Lin Zhang; Zhenggang Tang
abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. title: Interaction Latents as Actions for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Yuhang Zheng; Yujie Zang; Yuchen Liu; Yupeng Zheng; Zhennan Jiang; Zebin Xing
abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to coordinate not only where to move, but also how contact and force should evolve throughout an interaction. Yet most robot policies represent actions primarily as motion trajectories, using tactile signals as inputs or auxiliary prediction targets without explicitly encoding contact dynamics in the action representation. authors: Gennady Sidorov; Valerii Kornilov; Denis Grankin; Polina Fedotova; Aleksey Postnikov
abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. authors: Chenru Wen; Huajian Zeng; Haokai Ding; Jian Kang; Anqing Duan; Dawei Zhou
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. authors: Zhi Cao; Yining Hong; Jiaolong Yang; Yejin Choi; Li Fei-Fei; Jiajun Wu
abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. authors: Haodong Yang; Runhan Huang; Bowen Zhang; Iofai Lei; Zunzhe Zhang; Xiangcheng Zhang
abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. authors: Sitan Huang; Grace Gao
abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. authors: Jun Tian; Yingjie Niu; Ruo Chen; Hongyi Lin; Chao Li
abstract: Quadruped robots performing outdoor deliveries must interpret complex scenes, anticipate changes, and navigate in socially compliant ways. Robot demonstrations are costly to collect at the scale needed for generalization. Egocentric web videos offer abundant human navigation experience, but differences in viewpoint and motion make this experience difficult to transfer to robots. authors: Bingxin Xu; Wenrui Bao; Xinxin Liu; Jiawei Zhou; Yuzhang Shang; Emilio Ferrara
abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. authors: Mohammed Daba; Waleed Abdulrahman Saleh AlAkwa
abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as $π_{0.5}$, have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities by scaling behavior cloning across massive datasets. authors: Zhibo Duan; Hanlin Kong; Tianran Ma; Yuze Wu; Yuxuan Xu; Kenghou Hoi
abstract: Aerial mobile manipulation requires unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to traverse heterogeneous environments such as indoor and outdoor domains, and connect navigation with subsequent physical interaction within the same trajectories. authors: Changyeon Kim; Kimin Lee; Yashraj Narang; Yijie Guo
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. authors: Jun Xiao; Rui Ye; Dong Cao; Jinyu Gu; Ying Wang; Zhiliang Zhu
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. authors: Lei Yao; Qiao Feng; Mutian Tong; Qihao Yun; Lap-Pui Chau; Lingjie Liu
abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. authors: Wenzhan Li; Yiran Qin; Heng Zhou; Huirui Wang; Yulan Guo; Ruimao Zhang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. authors: Jingyuan Liu; Yunpeng Qing; Changxu Wei; Zhi Hou
abstract: Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle during execution. Reliable deployment therefore requires runtime monitoring that provides timely warnings of failure. authors: Jiaqi Fan; Rui Xu; Jiakun Xia; Xuyu Fan; Shuailei Ma; Yuefeng Wang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation by connecting visual perception and language instructions to action generation. authors: Zihan You; Zehua Fan; Wenqi Lyu; Aoqi Wang; Ni Wang; Yifei Yang
abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly use natural-language instructions to condition autonomous driving behavior. abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. authors: Junhyeong Go; Mingyu Jung; Woobin Im; Jongbin Ryu
abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction enable the extraction of temporally consistent 3D motion from RGB observations; however, current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models still predominantly rely on 2D image-text priors. authors: Zhi Han; Zihan Guo; Chenxi Zeng; Zicai Cui; Yue Xin; Ming Zhou
abstract: LLM agents increasingly control robots using VLA policies, perception models, and procedural knowledge. authors: Yuqi Ye; Caigao Jiang; Zhuonan Wang; Congyuan Pei; Chao Qu; Changhao Peng
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. authors: Ahaskar Kashyap; Jiawen Zong; Boyu Ma; Chuhao Zhou; Jingliang Li; Stefano V. Albrecht
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. authors: Wenjun Huang; Shenghao Fu; Yian Jin; Yang Ni; Yifan Li; Lichi Li
abstract: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, limiting their applicability in lights-out industrial environments where visible illumination may be unavailable. authors: Abdollah Pourasghari; Saeedeh Sadat Sadidpour; Mohammad Roustaei
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. title: $Δ$ Flow Matching for Robot Foundation Models
authors: Kuangji Zuo; Tuo An; Xinying Guo; Gen Li; Mengfei Zhao; Jiaqi Bai
abstract: Flow matching is a common generative recipe for robot foundation models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) generate action chunks, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally generate future visual states. Both start generation from a fixed Gaussian prior, despite temporal continuity between past and future states and actions. title: Verify, Act, Distill: Turning Test-Time Compute into Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka; Satoshi Yamamori; Jun Morimoto
abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. authors: Hieu D. Pham; Quoc-An Luong; Dung D. Le
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. title: Red-Teaming of Vision-Language-Action Models via Quality Diversity Environment Generation
authors: Shihan Zhao; Henry Chen; Ya-Chuan Hsu; Minjune Hwang; Siddharth Srikanth; Freddie Liang
abstract: A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in-distribution, they often fail under minor test-time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. authors: Chenghao Yue; Peiyan Li; Hao Wang; Lei Lv; Jiahao Chen; Huaping Liu
abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. authors: Zan Huang; Yibo Qiu; Kan Ding; Xuanping Zhang; Ao Tian; Ronald X Xu
abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. authors: Shutong Ding; Zhaoyang Liu; Yimiao Zhou; Jingya Wang; Jiayuan Gu; Ye Shi
abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). authors: Wenbo Yu; Jifan Li; Wenke Xia; Yuchen Li; Yizhuo Zhang; Pei Ren
abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. title: VLMs are Native Action Models: Unleashing the Manipulation Capabilities of VLMs with Explicit Action-Space Grounding
authors: Jingkun Yi; Shujie Zhang; Zirui Zhou; Haoxiao Wang; Haiyang Sun; Yuhang Dong
abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation
authors: Xiaomeng Ye; Krishna Jaganathan; Gyubeum Lim; Gunjan Chhablani; Muhammad Zubair Irshad; Zsolt Kira
abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $π_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. authors: Yuechen Luo; He Chong; Fang Li; Shaoqing Xu; Hexin Zhang; Ruiqi Zhang
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal; Abdelwahed Khamis; Mohammad Ali Armin; Lars Petersson
abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. authors: Xuhui Kang; Sung-Wook Lee; Yan Zhuang; Tianle Zhong; Yen-Ling Kuo
abstract: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Xule Gao; Xi Wang; Zehua Zang; Rui Wang; Changwen Zheng; Chuxiong Sun
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. authors: Junjie Lu; Chuheng Zhang; Yucen Wang; Yuhua Jiang; Xinyao Qin; Min Xu
abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
authors: Yilin Wu; Rutav Shah; Shuaiyi Huang; Sumedh A. Sontakke; Homanga Bharadhwaj; Andrea Bajcsy
abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. authors: Zhiyuan Xiang; Peidong Liu; Mingyang Li; Jiawei Li; Wenhow Li; Wenbo Ding
abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. authors: Faith Ogunwoye; Didar Seyidov; Konstantin Gubernatorov; Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. authors: Zipei Ma; Junzhe Jiang; Jiahui Zhang; Juntong Zhang; Chun Gu; Bozhou Zhang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. authors: Zile Zhong; Yuxin Du; Tao Lin; Haoxiao Wang; Wei Dai; Binhua Zuo
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. authors: Weiwei Chen; Chenghao Xu; Meiling Yu; Xu Yang; Cheng Deng
abstract: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. authors: Yang Wang; Ping Liu; Ruiyu Wang; Xuhua Chen; Lingfeng Zhang; Tao Zhang
abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. authors: Bahey Tharwat; Iman Nematollahi; Marvin Alles; Xingyuan Zhang; Akshay L Chandra; Abhinav Valada
abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. authors: Min Lin; Bokai Zhou; Jianqi Lin; Kaiyuan Yang; Yicheng Chang; Junjie Yu
abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. authors: Renbin Shu; Jing Yang; Xiangyuan You; Guolin Qiu; Yufei Xia; Yiming Zhu
abstract: Reliable manipulation requires policies that generalize across tasks, layouts, and object interactions. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained multimodal understanding with learned control, but their performance remains limited on unfamiliar task compositions. authors: Junmyeong Lee; Dongmin Shin; Min-Gyu Park; Wooseok Jeon; Inho Chang; Hae-Gon Jeon
abstract: Despite recent advances in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) for robotic manipulation, their performance remains sensitive to changes in camera configuration. The problem becomes more evident in cross-setup deployment, as reproducing the exact camera pose used for training is nearly impossible. Unlike fixed external views, wrist views are more challenging because the camera moves with the robot, causing even small mounting variations to alter fine-grained geometric cues. authors: Mert Albaba; Jens Beißwenger; Anna Manasyan; Daniel Marta; Michael J. Black; Wieland Brendel
abstract: Teaching a humanoid to follow instructions with its whole body runs into two obstacles. Its action space is large and tightly coupled: legs, arms, and fingers must move together while the robot keeps its balance, which makes joint-level actions hard to learn. authors: Boyao Han; Chen Shi; Jingjing Qian; ZhuoTan Tian; Li Jiang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful foundations for robotic manipulation, but their reliance on fixed camera configurations during training makes them brittle to changes in camera count or pose during deployment. authors: Zhaoyang Liu; Kun Jiang; Ziying Song; Diange Yang
abstract: VGGT provides a strong foundation for geometry-centric world models by recovering unified 3D scene geometry from visual observations. authors: Fazeng Li; Gan Sun; Hao Cheng; Weihong Ren; Yang Cong
abstract: Instruction following enables robots to perform diverse tasks specified in natural language, making it a fundamental capability for human-robot interaction. authors: Jason Chen; I-Chun Arthur Liu; Gaurav Sukhatme; Daniel Seita
abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation, with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. authors: Justin Tien-Smith; Matthew Pidden; Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. authors: Kyoungin Baik; Youngwoon Lee
abstract: Large-scale, diverse datasets have driven the success of LLMs and VLMs. But VLAs for robotics remain limited by the cost and complexity of real-world data collection. abstract: Embodied coding agents can combine modular robot skills with frozen end-to-end policies, yet effective composition requires anticipating which policy family will succeed in the current physical state. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent framework for complex robotic manipulation, building on the strong semantic understanding of pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs). authors: Yuchen Zhou; Jiacheng You; Weikang Wan; Weijun Dong; Yang Gao; Jiayuan Mao

authors: Hongyu Shi; Sen Zhao; Zuyu Zhang; Lifeng Shen; Ding Zou; Xinyu He
abstract: Latent reasoning enables vision-language-action (VLA) models to transform multimodal observations into task-relevant internal states before generating continuous robot actions. authors: Yuxin Chen; Senqiao Yang; Zixuan Wang; Jinhui Ye; Changsheng Lu; Pengguang Chen
abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires timely intervention to correct emerging deviations and restore progress after execution errors. authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran; Ruwan Wickramarachchi; Alessandro Oltramari; Jonathan Francis
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. authors: Houlong Xiong; Zhenqi Qiu; Zechen Wang; Suohang Zhang; Yiyu Ren; Wanting Xu
abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models generate action chunks for temporally coherent robot motion, but chunked control creates a fundamental closed-loop trade-off: long chunks provide smooth execution, whereas frequent replanning improves reactivity at the cost of action discontinuities. authors: Qing Huang; Yifei Yang; Ziqing Zou; Anzhe Chen; Zhenjie Zhu; Yufei Wei

authors: Yan Yang; Jikun Rong; Minzhao Zhu; Zheyi Zhao; Qirui Hu; Zihan Lan
abstract: Humanoid robots are a promising platform for general-purpose manipulation. authors: Qixuan Li; Yanhong Zhao; Jincheng Yu
abstract: Deploying frozen learned skills, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, in new environments requires identifying initiation configurations that support reliable execution. authors: Kairui Hu; Siyuan Hu; Fangzhou Hong; Zhaoxi Chen; Ziwei Liu
abstract: Most robot policies keep a model in the control loop: a VLA maps observations to actions, and an Agent Harness, such as Agent-as-Policy or Harness VLA queries a VLM for decision making at run time. authors: Ruicheng Zhang; Kaiwen Shen; Jiaqi Hou; Shuhan Yang; Junchao Huang; Kewei Zhang
abstract: Generalized referring expression segmentation (GRES) requires dynamically balancing high-level semantics for identifying a variable number of language-specified referents with fine-grained visual evidence for precise boundary delineation. title: CAPABLE: Capability-Aware Policy Adaptation via Behavioral Latent Encoding
authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar; Mohammad Dehghani Tezerjani; Deyuan Qu; Zhiyuan Gao; Yanxiang Zhan; Jeroen Schafer
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies assume the embodiment on which they were trained and can fail when a joint fault changes how commanded actions are physically executed. Existing fault-recovery methods often require task-specific retraining, fault labels, explicit diagnosis, or privileged embodiment information. authors: Gokul Puthumanaillam; Tao Sun; Elie Aljalbout; Moritz Reuss; Zhaoshuo Li; Fabio Ramos
abstract: The prevailing approach to improving robot foundation models (RFMs) relies on larger models, more robot demonstrations, and costly training at scale. abstract: Shortcut learning is a prevalent issue in robot learning. The limited diversity of robot demonstration datasets can mislead policies into exploiting spurious correlations between tasks and irrelevant features, such as viewpoint or background. authors: Yanjiang Guo; Haodong Yan; Zhide Zhong; Zhongru Zhang; Qingyuan Yang; Qingzhou Lu
abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as an important class of generalist robot policies, aiming to transfer video prediction priors to action learning. However, we find that existing WAMs frequently produce incorrect motion predictions in open-ended environment, leading to erroneous actions. authors: Yeonseo Lee; Hyosup Shin; Guebin Hwang; Sungho Jo
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are effective at understanding what task to perform, but provide limited control over how it should be executed, such as moving quickly or slowly. authors: Zirun Zhou; Jingfeng Zhang; HaoChuan Xu; Xizhe Zhang; Elliott Wen; Jing Sun
abstract: Backdoored vision-language-action (VLA) policies can preserve benign task performance while producing malicious actions when a trigger appears. authors: Jingya Wang; Dehao Zhang; Shuai Wang; Malu Zhang; Yang Yang; Haizhou Li
abstract: ANN-to-SNN conversion offers a practical route toward energy-efficient spiking Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by bypassing the substantial cost of training large-scale SNNs from scratch. authors: Jiho Lee; Jeongeun Park; Heayoun Choi; Taekyung Kim; Eunwoo Kim
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. title: RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
authors: Mimo Shirasaka; Takehiko Ohkawa; Takuya Okubo; Nicola Scianca; Tatsuya Matsushima; Kei Ota
abstract: Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. authors: Mikey Watts; Yuchen Cui
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are strikingly sensitive to instruction phrasing and do not inherit the language robustness of the vision-language models they are built on. authors: Yonghoon Dong; Minsung Yoon; Jaehyuk Kim; Jungwoo Park; Changyeon Kim; Jinwoo Shin
abstract: Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. authors: Yifan Wu; Qin Li; Nan Min; Guojin Zhong; Haoyu Zhao; Zhiyuan Li
abstract: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. authors: Gengze Zhou; Yicong Hong; Jiazhao Zhang; Xunyi Zhao; Jian Zhou; Zixing Lei
abstract: Language models trained with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning can generalize knowledge through reasoning, express precise actions, and pursue goals over many steps, raising the ceiling on what an embodied agent can understand and decide. authors: Haoru Li; Jinmei Liu; Zhiyong Wang; Xiaoming Li; Zhenhong Sun; Daoyi Dong
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through closed-loop experience, yet generalization beyond the fine-tuning distribution remains limited. authors: Wei Huang; Bohan Zhang; Chenzhi Liu; Isabella Liu; Shuai Yang; Weian Mao
abstract: Real-time robot control demands enough visual history to infer motion and task progress, but processing that history can delay action. We present Long-WAM, a model-system framework for scaling the context of causal world-action models under real-time control constraints. authors: Yuchen Zhu; Chenyi Xu; Yulin Zhang; Gang Xu; Wentao Zhu
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict masked or future observations in representation space, offering a natural source of predictive latents for vision-language-action (VLA) models. authors: Xingtai Gui; Yucheng Zhou; Dongqian Guo; Jiahao Gong; Feiyang Tan; Jianbing Shen
abstract: Vision-language-action~(VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. authors: Python Song; Zhixuan Liang; Kelsey Fu; Mengdi Wang; Junfeng Yang; Shilong Liu
abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. authors: Theodor Wulff; Angelo Cangelosi
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models are designed to generalise across environments and task descriptions, raising the question of whether their action generation actually depends on the language instruction, or whether they largely rely on visual cues and superficial correlations. authors: Xiaoyi Pang; Haoyue Feng; Quanxin Shou; Yikun Miao; Zhengyang Yan; Song Guo
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical physical environments, yet their adversarial robustness remains poorly understood. Existing attacks typically assume white-box access or rely on surrogate VLAs, which rarely holds in real-world deployments. authors: Thinh D. Le; Son T. Nguyen; Duong Q. Nguyen; Dung D. Le; Ngo Anh Vien; H. Nguyen-Xuan
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved impressive results in robotic manipulation and ground-mobile navigation, yet language-conditioned control of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart warehouses remains largely unexplored, hindered by the lack of benchmarks that jointly provide continuous low-level flight actions, fine-grained natural-language target descriptions, and realistic industrial environments. authors: Yuan Xu; Yixiang Chen; Qisen Ma; Jiabing Yang; Peiyan Li; Kai Wang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. abstract: Portable mobile-manipulation demonstrations can help alleviate data scarcity for embodied intelligence, but obtaining reliable, low-cost, and robot-free motion supervision from RGB observations remains challenging. authors: Owen Du; Yang Yue; Jie Zhang; Jiaqi Pi; Chi Bene Chen; Gao Huang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. authors: Zijia Chen; Yuenan Hou; Yu Li; Weijie Li; Li Liu
abstract: Network pruning can reduce parameter redundancy in robotic policies. authors: Shangyuan Yuan; Xinda Qi; Yujiang Pu; Wenliang Guo; Xiaobo Tan
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly rely on diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads to generate continuous robot actions. authors: Hojoon Son; Fan Zhang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a major paradigm for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN). authors: Jicong Ao; Shuhan Jiang; Yuling Zhong; Yanwen Liu; Yuhan Gao; Jiangyuan Zhao
abstract: The ability to interact with articulated objects is essential for embodied intelligent systems, but collecting large-scale real-world demonstrations for these interactions remains challenging due to the precise contact and constraint-following motions involved. authors: Kaixi Feng; Guoheng Sun; Ang Li
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. authors: Jaeyoung Lee; Jiyeon Koo; Taehwa Kim; Yerin Cha; Andrew Jaeyong Choi

abstract: Scaling robotic foundation models requires diverse training data and reliable evaluation environments. authors: Lilika Makabe; Heecheol Kim; Yasuyuki Matsushita
abstract: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching have been increasingly adopted in vision-language-action (VLA) policies for their ability to capture diverse behaviors, including multiple valid action sequences under the same observation and instruction. authors: Xilun Zhang; Maggie Wang; Erik Bauer; Hong-Xing Yu; Huang Huang; Jiajun Wu
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained on large datasets are capable within their training domains, yet they still fail to generalize to the variety of situations a robot meets in real-world deployment. abstract: While vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly, running them at every control step remains expensive. authors: Zexi Zhang; Zecheng Zhu; Zidong Chen; Zulkhuu Tuya; Stephen James

authors: Ahin Lee; Jinwoo Seo; Youngsoo Jang; Taesik Gong
abstract: Visual disruptions can arise while a robot is executing a task, leaving a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to respond without knowing the disruption type or timing. abstract: Dense affordance supervision is an appealing auxiliary signal for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, yet naively co-training an affordance head can severely damage instruction following. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models serve as unified policies for robotic manipulation, yet their expensive inference forces robots to pause between policy calls, resulting in stop-and-go execution that interrupts smooth motion and prolongs task completion. title: What the Guard Misses, the Robot Executes: Implied Harm in VLA Instructions
authors: Sripad Karne; Arjun Balaji
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) act on instructions without being able to refuse, so screening harmful requests falls to monitors. We test whether these monitors catch ordinary robot tasks requested for harmful reasons, holding the task fixed while varying only how explicitly the intent is stated. $π_{0.5}$ completes the task at every level of explicitness, as often as for harmless controls. authors: Jaemin Kim; Jiahn Kim; Taesik Gong
abstract: Adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models to deployment-time distribution shifts is important for reliable robotic operation, but conventional first-order adaptation can exceed the memory budget of inference-oriented deployment platforms. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a forward-only alternative with inference-level memory, but accurate gradient estimation requires many perturbation queries, making naive ZO prohibitively slow for large VLA models. title: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models
authors: Xiaodong Wang; Tianle Li; Chuanxin Song; Junliang Xie; Zhanmi Zhong; Suiying Wu
abstract: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. title: Recursive Video In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot
authors: Wenrui Bao; Xinxin Liu; Bingxin Xu; Yuzhang Shang
abstract: LLM agents that orchestrate frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies improve across episodes through text memory, which records what the agent did but not how the task is done. title: PlaySuite: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Interactive Visual Intelligence
authors: Dheeraj Varghese; Anna Vettoruzzo; Walter Simoncini; Michelle Lorena Acevedo Callejas; Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani; Kristof Meding
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models yield strong performance on static perception and reasoning benchmarks, yet such evaluations largely overlook a central aspect of intelligence: acting competently in dynamic environments over extended time horizons. We introduce PlaySuite, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating interactive visual intelligence across more than 5K open-source video games curated from PyWeek and itch.io. authors: Jungho Kim; Hongjae Shin; Seunghoon Yu; Heecheol Yoo; Myeongjun Kim; Jiyong Oh
abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end driving requires continuous rollouts that reveal how earlier decisions affect subsequent driving. However, existing benchmarks evaluate only short segments and fail to capture later consequences. Ambiguous directional commands also obscure the intended navigation objective. title: OGAM: Connecting Systematic Testing to Runtime Assurance through Object-Grounded Attention Monitoring for VLA Policies
authors: Haki Darwish; Xiangyu Yin; Changwen Li; Rongjie Yan; Francisco Gomes de Oliveira Neto; Chih-Hong Cheng
abstract: Benchmarks expose vision-language-action (VLA) policies to few canonical instructions, while exhaustive deployment testing is impossible. We introduce Object-Grounded Attention Monitoring (OGAM), connecting systematic testing to runtime assurance: testing reveals attention divergence between successful and failed executions, and OGAM uses this signal to stop failures beyond the finite suite. title: How (and How Not) to Use Data Augmentation in VLA Post-Training
authors: Bram Grooten; Joaquin Vanschoren
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models currently demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of real-world robotics tasks. However, they often still lack the generalization ability to handle large visual out-of-distribution shifts. Post-training of VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to benefit robustness, but significant room for improvement remains. title: Encoded but Not in Control: Revealing the Grounding Gap in Vision-Language Robot Policies
authors: Shaohan Jiang; Jiahang Cao; Qiduo He; Fengting Deng; Kun Wu; Jingkai Sun
abstract: Instruction following is central to language-conditioned robot policies: language should determine what to do when the same scene permits multiple valid actions. Yet successful execution alone cannot establish whether a policy follows the instruction or infers the task from the scene. We study this ambiguity through scene-preserving instruction interventions, using valid target substitutions, arbitrary nouns, and unrelated sentences while holding the scene fixed. authors: Xinnuo Xu
abstract: This paper asks whether VLA generalization is grounded in a global understanding of objects' physical properties that enables policies to adapt their motion to unseen setups, or if policies simply replay the motions they've learnt that happen to succeed in new setups. authors: Yulong Yang; Fan Wu; Christine Allen-Blanchette; Amit Chakraborty
abstract: Diffusion and VLA policies for manipulation are often deployed through downstream impedance controllers. The stiffness and damping gains of these controllers affect task success, yet are commonly inherited from data collection rather than selected for the deployed policy. authors: Shen Ruan; Wenchang Gao; Jin Wang; Siao Liu;  Zhaxizhuoma; Dongchun Ren
abstract: Post-training quantization has been shown to preserve VLA performance under standard evaluation conditions, but whether it preserves the full-precision model's robustness and generalization remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically study the robustness and generalization of post-quantized VLA policies under environmental disturbances. title: Arm-wise Compositional Generalization in Dual-Arm Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zaibin Zhang; Binghao Ran; Yuhan Wu; Zhongbo Zhang; Yifan Wang; Junwei Jiang
abstract: Generalization in multi-arm collaboration can be studied as composing familiar atomic skills in new ways across arms. However, existing evaluations offer limited insight into which training and architectural choices support this ability under different coordination requirements. We introduce \textbf{ACG-Bench}, a benchmark for \emph{Arm-wise Compositional Generalization} that provides a common testbed for studying skill recomposition in dual-arm policies. authors: Tianjun Shi; Haotian Xiong; Ziyu Gong; Qi Lu; Li Li
abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate vision-language models and is especially useful for vision-language-action (VLA) inference, where many visual tokens must be processed before predicting robot actions. Existing pruning methods usually estimate which tokens can be pruned based on attention scores or feature diversity, retaining tokens that are either highly attended or visually different from others. title: When Does Retrieval Help? A Study of In-Context Adaptation in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zixuan Liu; Joris Köster; Zizhan Zheng; Siavash Khajavi
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential as generalist robot policies, but adapting them to unseen tasks often requires costly parameter updates. Recent work such as RICL introduces in-context adaptability by retrieving expert demonstrations based on the current VLA observation and providing them as additional context at test time. authors: Yifan Li; Jiaxu Wang; Dongming Wu; Yicheng Jiang; Ryan Ji; Xiangyu Yue
abstract: Most vision-language-action models represent future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, tying temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise representation wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision required for contact-rich manipulation. authors: Hyemin Yang; Wooseong Jeong; Giwon Lee; Kuk-Jin Yoon
abstract: Dual-system Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models improve real-time robotic control by pairing a slow, reasoning-capable generalist with a fast specialist action expert. However, existing methods invoke the generalist at a fixed frequency, ignoring the fact that decision-making complexity varies throughout a rollout. authors: Shizuo Tian; Haodong Luo; Yutong Li; Yuebing Song; Yunxin Liu; Yuanchun Li
abstract: Rapid adaptation to a new environment requires a robot to acquire useful knowledge about local objects, states, and interactions from limited experience. Systems that combine a reasoning agent with a frozen vision-language-action model (VLA) can adapt through execution feedback and memory, making the choice of experience central to their effectiveness. authors: Hyun Song; Kangmin Kim; Loren Jinsoo Um; Minhui Han; Jaehyeok Park; Taewan Cho
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models encode semantic information from vision-language pretraining, but manipulation also requires precise spatial reasoning. We present GeoBridge-VLA, a two-stage method for learning geometric features from a pretrained VLA's frozen visual encoder and using them for action prediction. authors: Yuheng Na; Zhide Zhong; Junjie He; Junfeng Li; Haodong Yan; Jiaan Wang
abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on current observations and lose task-relevant evidence once it leaves view, limiting performance on long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. Existing efforts incorporate compressed historical features or sparse visual keyframes. authors: Seongheon Park; Heecheol Kim; Shulin Tian; Lilika Makabe; Namiko Saito; Katsushi Ikeuchi
abstract: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. authors: Seonghun Jung; Sieun Moon; Jiyoung Jeong; Jimin Lee; Jaehyuk Huh
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate multimodal observations into low-level robot actions. During robot operation, each control period sets an inference deadline, and overruns leave the robot acting on stale observations, reducing task success. Meeting this deadline motivates on-device or nearby edge execution, where a single robot requires batch-1 inference outside the design point of LLM serving systems. authors: Tu Nguyen; Matthieu Zimmer; Vu Anh Vu; Ziyi Wang; Jannik Hammel Nielsen; Xuebing Zhou
abstract: A safe action is not necessarily a viable one. A frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy can favor a locally admissible move that leaves no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility-likelihood gap: likelihood ranks the next move, while feasibility depends on the futures it leaves open. authors: Peilin Wang; Feng Shiyang; Hongfu Gao; Cencheng Zhao; Di Yuan; Hui Chen
abstract: Recursive computation repeatedly compresses or reuses intermediate states, creating a simple tension: information that must remain useful across longer recursive paths is also exposed to more opportunities for loss before reaching the final prediction. title: WasserMan: Benchmark for Underwater Manipulation Policy Learning
authors: Danil Belov; Artem Erkhov; Sergei Parsegov; Pavel Osinenko
abstract: Underwater manipulation couples visual decisions, contact forces and a thruster-controlled floating base. We introduce WasserMan, to our knowledge the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base underwater contact manipulation. It provides ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle-arm platforms, a bimanual configuration and underwater dynamics. Nine tasks have learned-policy evaluations. authors: Mousumi Das; Aditeya Prajapati; Abrar Anwar; Jesse Thomason
abstract: Robot manipulation systems using Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model backbones typically use just one VLA for task execution. However, individual VLAs do not perform well across different task states and environments. We introduce a framework for dynamically composing multiple VLA policies during execution: StepWise Action Policy Routing (SWAP). authors: Jiuzhou Lei; Chang Liu; Dayou Li; Zhiyuan Zhang; Xiao Liang; Yu She
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability. To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters. authors: Yanqiao Chen; Yuhan Rui; Dongsheng Hou; Zijie Nie; Yutong Wan; Qi Hao
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. authors: Yi Wang; Yang Yang; Guangqi Xu; Sumin Lin; Ning Kang; Pengxiang Lu
abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires inferring task-relevant states from past interactions when the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the appropriate action. Despite progress in benchmarking memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models, application-oriented tasks requiring history-dependent semantic inference remain underrepresented. authors: Zhe Tao; Feiran Wang; Gaowen Liu; Ramana Rao Kompella; Yan Yan
abstract: Robots need to anticipate how their actions will change the world, since manipulation success hinges on the resulting contacts and object motions. authors: I-Chun Arthur Liu; Jason Chen; Gaurav S. Sukhatme; Daniel Seita
abstract: Three-dimensional perception is critical for robotic manipulation, particularly for high-precision tasks, as recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB observations is inherently ill-posed. authors: Elizaveta Semenyakina; Ivan Snegirev; Mikhail Kiselev; Miguel Altamirano Cabrera; Artem Lykov; Hajira Amjad
abstract: Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual feedback degrades under closure occlusion. authors: Chen Yang; Linzhe Shi; Changjie Wu; Hang Zhang; Ronghan Chen; Lingjun Zhang
abstract: Tactile sensing provides essential contact information for robotic manipulation, yet incorporating it into pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging. authors: Rhythm Syed; Jean Mercat; Sedrick Keh; Kushal Arora; Paarth Shah; Aykut Onol
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit strong semantic grounding from pretrained vision-language backbones but are typically optimized for predicting actions rather than future observations. authors: Xingxin He; Yuxuan Jiang; Haonan Zhang; Chuhan Cui; Kaile Li; Zhongxing Zheng
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often require costly real-world demonstrations to adapt to contact-rich manipulation tasks, particularly when generalization across object placements is needed. authors: Chenxi Li; Zhangrui Zhao; Rui Li; Yuan Gao; Kehui Liu; Jiarui Li
abstract: A key challenge in bringing embodied intelligence into the real world is transferring capabilities from simulation to reality and enabling agents to continually adapt after deployment. authors: Seunghun Lee; Kyuhwan Shim; Yeogyeong Song; Seung Hwan Kim; Sihaeng Lee; Byoung-Tak Zhang
abstract: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale vision-language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. authors: Chunghyun Park; Beomjun Kim; Seungcheol Park; Heeseung Kwon; Yashu Shukla; Seunghoon Sim
abstract: World action models jointly learn to forecast world dynamics and predict robot actions, such that the learned internal world dynamics guide accurate actions. authors: Chenzhi Liu; Yue Zhang; Jiehong Lin; Jianan Wang; Bo Wang; Zhongrui Wang
abstract: Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. authors: Pingrui Zhang; Yu Zhang; Pengyuan Wu; Bin Wang; Haoming Song; Xianqiang Gao
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable advances in robotic manipulation, yet their zero-shot generalization under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions remains limited. authors: Sangwu Park; Yeonjun In; Wonjoong Kim; Sungwon Kim; Sein Kim; Chanyoung Park
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform diverse manipulation tasks, but task success in existing rigid-body benchmarks does not indicate whether they preserve objects. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging. abstract: Before deploying runtime recovery for a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy, one must establish that an intervention improves success beyond ordinary run-to-run variation and that its complexity adds value over a simple action. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide strong behavioral priors for robotic manipulation, yet efficiently adapting them to downstream tasks remains challenging. authors: Samuel Zhen; Siwon Jo; Yanze Zhang; Wenhao Luo
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generalizable robotic manipulation, but their deployment in the real world remains challenging due to potential collisions involving different parts of the robot, manipulated objects, and the surrounding environment. authors: Sofya Konstantinova; Miguel Altamirano Cabrera; Artem Lykov; Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies enable diverse robotic manipulation but can fail during execution without recognizing their own errors. Human observers provide complementary signals, as unexpected robot behavior can trigger rapid vocal, facial, or verbal reactions before failure is completed. abstract: In this paper, we study how to achieve one-step action generation in Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs), aiming to overcome the high inference latency of multi-step flow matching. authors: Sophie Higham; Riccardo Andrea Izzo; Matteo Matteucci; Alessandro Suglia
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). authors: Kyochul Jang; Seohyeon Park; Ohchul Kwon; Sangjun Park; Junhyeok Choi; Seungyeop Yi
abstract: As robotic hardware and learning methods advance, humanoids need tools to perform tasks beyond their inherent physical limits. authors: Ruiyang Si; Jianxin Bi; Shunyu Yang; Rui Ni; Wenbo Huang; Qiang Wang
abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents can control robots through visual feedback and action primitives, but repeated LLM calls and redundant observations incur substantial token overhead. authors: Hanchu Zhou; Dechen Gao; Hang Wang; Brendan Lynch; Boqi Zhao; Qiyao Ma
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. authors: Edward W. Staley; Connor O. Pyles; Rahul Hingorani; Frank Camargo; Griffin Milsap; Jared Markowitz
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely strongly on language for describing task information, despite having multimodal inputs. authors: Zhugang Liu; Kaichuang Zhang; Jinman Zhang; Pu Sun; Martha Asare; Jose Hernandez
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation, offering new opportunities for automation in additive manufacturing (AM). However, deployment in AM remains challenging because adapting these models to unseen robot embodiments is costly, and performance can degrade under environment changes. authors: Yijie Zhu; Rui Shao; Jie He; Wei Li; Bo Zhao; Yelin Wang
abstract: Predictive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to improve robotic manipulation via future observation or world dynamics forecasting. However, existing approaches often fail to realize this potential and underperform direct action prediction models. We argue that these limitations stem from modality misalignment between observations and actions, together with joint optimization conflicts that drive learning away from an action-centric objective. authors: Ziyan Jiang; Jingbo Yang; Jiabao Ji; Yujian Liu; Qiucheng Wu; Tommi Jaakkola

authors: Chongyang Xu; Zhao Wu; Jin Chen; Yiming Jiang; Jinhui Ye; Yuming Jiang

authors: Di Wu; Rongtian Shen; Ping Liu; Yan Shen; Zhenhan Yin; Shun Zuo
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models face a timing gap between low-rate inference and high-rate robot execution. authors: Chuyao Fu; Xiaowei Chi; Yuhan Rui; Yu-kai Wang; Zezhong Qian; Xiaojie Zhang
abstract: A common approach to world-model simulation for vision-language-action (VLA) systems is to predict future RGB observations and then re-encode them into policy inputs, introducing an indirect interface between simulation and downstream policy execution. authors: Ali Alrasheed; Basim Azam; Naveed Akhtar
abstract: World models offer a promising way to help robots understand how the physical world evolves and plan complex behaviours through imagination. abstract: Mastering robot manipulation skills via reinforcement learning (RL) remains largely sample-inefficient. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bridge multimodal understanding and robotic control, advancing the dominant paradigm for embodied intelligence. abstract: We present PrefPI (Preference-Guided Policy Iteration), an iterative framework for steering pretrained generative robot policies using only relative preferences over self-generated trajectories. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models based on generative frameworks, such as Flow Matching, have recently achieved impressive performance in robotic manipulation. authors: Yatharth Agarwal; Vijay Raghunathan
abstract: A vision-language-action (VLA) policy can finish a manipulation task while knocking over objects unrelated to it, so task success alone does not show that the policy is safe to deploy in clutter. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize broadly across robotic manipulation tasks, but complex environments require balancing task success with unintended contact. authors: Songhua Yang; Ziyu Liu; Yuanwei Liu; Xuetao Li; Xuanye Fei; He Huang
abstract: Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have revolutionized robotic manipulation by seamlessly integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation in an end-to-end learning framework. authors: Yize Liu; Ke Wang; Mac Schwager; Yiqing Xu; Jiajun Wu

authors: Haoyuan Deng; Jiebin Liu; Tengxiao Zhang; Langning Yan; Hongye Cao; Ziwei Wang

abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in static tasks, they struggle in dynamic environments where objects are in motion (e.g., conveyor belt manipulation). authors: Hongcheng Gao; Jingjing Zhou; Zelin Zheng; Shijia Ge; Jay Zhu; Yazhe Wang

authors: Rongyu Zhang; Ruizhi Fan; Yunfan Lou; Hengyu Fang; Shenli Zheng; Chenrui Wu
abstract: Vision-language-action and world-action models are increasingly popular, yet remain bottlenecked by physical interaction data that is scarce, institutionally siloed, and task-heterogeneous. authors: Zhe Sun; Ziyi Luo; Yehao Lu; Lei Zhou; Xi Li
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving rely heavily on successful expert demonstrations, leaving model-specific failures underexploited. abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models are highly effective for generalist robot manipulation, yet their reliance on computationally expensive VLM encoding and multi-step iterative action generation imposes a significant latency bottleneck. abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with action heads for robot control. authors: Mingle Jiang; Rui Xu; Yunke Wang; Chang Xu
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, but they are typically developed and evaluated with all camera streams available throughout task execution. abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models using discrete action tokens have proven effective for controling robotic arms on manipulation tasks.
